preamble.summary: LXX Ruth tracks the Hebrew text closely. The translators preserved the book's narrative rhythm and key institutional vocabulary (kinsman-redeemer, levirate, gleaning) with only minor Greek stylistic adjustments. The most interesting LXX choice in Ruth is the rendering of go'el as anchisteus — a technical term for 'the next of kin,' the one on whom inherited legal obligations fall. This choice had a long afterlife in Hellenistic Jewish legal thought and in early Christian uses of 'kinsman-redeemer' language for Christ.
preamble.notable_variants: The anchisteus vocabulary for the kinsman-redeemer throughout chapters 3 and 4; the 'under whose wings you have come to take refuge' imagery at 2:12 that Jesus picks up at Matthew 23:37; the levirate legal procedures of 4:5–7; and the closing genealogy that Matthew 1:5 inherits to list Ruth in the Messianic line.
preamble.theological_legacy: LXX Ruth's anchisteus vocabulary did not pass directly into NT Christology — the NT prefers lytrōtēs and agchistēs-less phrasing — but it shaped the Hellenistic Jewish legal concept of kinship-redemption that Paul's 'adoption' (huiothesia) language presupposes. Ruth's inclusion in Jesus' genealogy at Matthew 1:5 is the single most visible theological consequence of the book's reception: a Moabite woman, preserved by the kinsman-redeemer institution, becomes an ancestor of the Messiah.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὁ λαός σου λαός μου καὶ ὁ θεός σου θεός μου
renderings.mt_rendering: Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God
renderings.lxx_rendering: Your people shall be my people, and your God my God
notes: Ruth's covenant-declaration to Naomi has the same structural form — 'X of yours shall be X of mine' — that appears in covenant-incorporation language across the LXX (compare Hosea 2:23 LXX, quoted in Rom 9:25 and 1 Pet 2:10: "I will say to 'Not My People,' 'you are my people'").

The LXX preserves the terse symmetry of the Hebrew ('your people my people, your God my God') without expansion. The phrase circulated in Hellenistic Jewish proselyte discourse as a model confession of a Gentile joining the covenant community.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὑπὸ τὰς πτέρυγας αὐτοῦ ἐφ᾽ ὃν ἦλθες πεποιθέναι ὑπ᾽ αὐτόν
renderings.mt_rendering: under whose wings you have come to take refuge
renderings.lxx_rendering: under whose wings you have come to trust
notes: Boaz's blessing on Ruth — that she has come under YHWH's wings for refuge — uses the Greek pterygas autou ('his wings') that Jesus will echo at Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34: 'how often I would have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings (hypo tas pterygas).'

The wings-of-refuge image threads through the Psalms (17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 61:4, 63:7, 91:4) in its LXX form, where it accumulates an eschatological and Messianic charge. Jesus' Jerusalem-lament reaches back through the whole LXX mother-bird-and-wings tradition to claim that role for himself.
The LXX's pepoithenai ('to trust, to be confident') renders the Hebrew l-chasot ('to take refuge') with faith-vocabulary that anticipates Pauline pistis language.

LXX Ruth renders go'el as anchisteus — 'the nearest of kin, the one next in line of inheritance.' The Greek word is legally technical: the anchisteus is the person on whom inherited obligations (land redemption, levirate marriage, blood vengeance) fall by kinship order.

The Pentateuch's go'el (Lev 25:25, 25:48–49; Num 35:12) is rendered with the same anchisteus word-field. LXX Ruth therefore keeps the legal vocabulary of the Pentateuch intact in Greek, which is why Ruth reads as a Torah case study in Greek as in Hebrew.

Christian theology of Christ as 'kinsman-redeemer' develops, in part, from the Latin propinquus and redemptor (Vulgate Ruth) rather than directly from the LXX anchisteus. But the LXX established that go'el denotes a kinship-based legal relationship rather than a pure commercial redemption.

renderings.mt_reading: וּמֵאֵת רוּת הַמּוֹאֲבִיָּה אֵשֶׁת־הַמֵּת קָנִיתָ לְהָקִים שֵׁם־הַמֵּת עַל־נַחֲלָתוֹ
renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ παρὰ Ρουθ τῆς Μωαβίτιδος γυναικὸς τοῦ τεθνηκότος καὶ αὐτὴν κτήσασθαι δεῖ σε ὥστε ἀναστῆσαι τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ τεθνηκότος ἐπὶ τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the wife of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of the dead man upon his inheritance
renderings.lxx_rendering: from Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, you must also acquire her, so as to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance
notes: The LXX's anastēsai to onoma ('raise up the name') uses the verb anistēmi — the same verb that becomes the standard NT word for resurrection. The levirate custom's 'raising the name of the dead' is, in Greek, literally a 'standing up' of the dead name over his inheritance.

This is not a direct theological typology for resurrection, but the verbal overlap shaped Hellenistic Jewish imagination about the relation between lineage-continuation, land-inheritance, and divine raising-up of the dead.
Matthew 22:24 has the Sadducees cite the levirate law (Deut 25) to Jesus in terms drawn from LXX Ruth and Deuteronomy — exanastēsei sperma tō adelphō autou ('shall raise up seed for his brother').

renderings.lxx_reading: ὑπελύετο ὁ ἀνὴρ τὸ ὑπόδημα αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐδίδου τῷ πλησίον αὐτοῦ
renderings.mt_rendering: a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party
renderings.lxx_rendering: a man would remove his sandal and give it to his neighbor
notes: The sandal-removal custom for confirming a legal transaction is preserved in Greek with the neighbor-vocabulary plēsion — the same word that carries the Leviticus 19:18 love-your-neighbor command into LXX form.

John the Baptist's disclaimer at John 1:27 ('the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie') may evoke LXX Ruth's sandal-transfer indirectly: the Baptist refuses to stand in the kinsman-redeemer position vis-à-vis the Messiah.

renderings.mt_reading: וַתִּקְרֶאנָה לוֹ הַשְּׁכֵנוֹת שֵׁם … הוּא אֲבִי־יִשַׁי אֲבִי דָוִד
renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἐκάλεσαν αὐτοῦ αἱ γείτονες ὄνομα … οὗτος πατὴρ Ιεσσαι πατρὸς Δαυιδ
renderings.mt_rendering: The neighbor women gave him a name … He was the father of Jesse, the father of David
renderings.lxx_rendering: And the neighbors named him … this is the father of Jesse, the father of David
notes: The closing genealogy of LXX Ruth supplies the framework Matthew 1:5 inherits: 'Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, Obed fathered Jesse, Jesse fathered David.' Matthew preserves the Greek name-forms (Booz, Iobed, Iessai, Dauid) of the LXX.

Luke 3:32 gives the same genealogy in reverse (ascending). Both evangelists are reading LXX Ruth 4 as the authoritative record of David's non-Israelite ancestry. The inclusion of Ruth (and implicitly Rahab from Josh 2 / 6) among the Messianic ancestors is pointedly an inclusion of Gentile-outsider women in the line of the king.
